d:
This text is one of the rarest, earliest examples of lolicon eroguro novels and works by , whom was behind many imprints and associations of the lolicon boom. With that said, this work was illustrated by Yuu Shiozawa (Shiozawa Yoshiaki), who, while at the time amateur, was very close with members of this camp. The actual book is only 3 x 3 inches and stapled. Featuring novels and works surrounding Sunrise mecha shows such as Xabungle, Acrobnch and Ideon, this work also features a very early depiction of futanari via Rag Ulao from Zabungle, Kitty Kitten's decapitation and tentacle sex gore via Reika Landau / Randolf from Acrobunch.

This particular work is a compilation of erotic short story works by Hōka Menoshima (billed as Hawken Miroshima in English), who was behind the imprint Transvester (トランスベスター), which was mentioned by Yoshihiro Yonezawa wrote about in 1982 in one of his doujinshi pick-up articles published in Lemon People. The circle seems to be associated with Transvester via the following: "started self-published / doujin activities in May 1981. Began presiding over Transvester (トランスベスター) in the spring of the following year.) Akihiko Kasajima is listed as the publisher, but its uncertain as to who this may be. The circle seems to be associated with Transvester and its publishing imprint Suisō.

https://varishangout.com/index.php?threads/lolicon-history-fusion-product-lolita-bishoujo-special-edition-translation.1003/page-7#post-39319 - translated by Taruby.

As with other works of this era, a common thread is common via the final bylines.

"Regarding misbound or missing pages: even if the fault is ours, we accept absolutely no responsibility. Also, please be sure to send letters and razor blades or similar items by sealed mail."

The usage of sending razorblades via mail was a (often referred to in subculture contexts as カミソリ送付 / kamisori sōfu or カミソリレター / kamisori retā) via the mail was a visceral, highly recognized form of malicious death threat, intense harassment, or extreme expression of fan rage. All the same, Otaku seemingly seem to have adopted it as a friendly way to say they enjoyed the work as well.
